+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply a _replace_table to the str s. A merge whose two tokens are not both
+    in s cannot match, so its replace (a full scan of s) is skipped: present
+    holds every char that is or was in s (a superset of the current chars).
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    for ps, c, a, b in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            t = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(t) != len(s):
+                present.add(c)
+                s = t
+    return s

actions.reason: Skipping merges whose pair tokens are absent kept outputs identical, but encode_ir went to ratio 1.0112, about 1.1% worse. Building the presence set and running the per-merge checks costs more than the skipped str.replace scans save. Not enough budget left to try a different approach.

journal.text:
I read regex.py, basic.py, base.py, gpt4.py and lineage_bench.py, then edited basic.py and regex.py. The idea was to skip merges whose pair tokens are absent from the current text, so encode avoids str.replace scans that cannot match.

Outputs stayed identical and both builds passed, but the sandbox evaluation rejected it. encode_ir went from 420854316 to 425561936, ratio 1.0112 against a required 0.9900. train_ir went from 377228428 to 377992822, ratio 1.0020. I gave up without submitting a candidate.

My read is that building the presence set and doing the per-merge membership checks costs more than the str.replace calls it skips. str.replace on a miss is already a fast C scan, so filtering in Python loses. The replace-table approach looks close to its floor on this kind of pruning.

Next I want to cut Python-level per-merge work instead of adding to it. One option is batching merges by rank, or reducing how many merges each chunk iterates. I should also profile encode_ir first to see where the instructions actually go.
